title: Identify the legislative requirements for perishable produce exportation

lessons.title: Regulatory bodies and registration requirements
lessons.html:
Who regulates perishable produce exports

A manager in the export chain must know which bodies have legal authority, what each one controls, and what registrations must be in place before the season starts. Missing a registration can close a market to a farm for a whole season.

BodyMain regulatory function
National Department of AgricultureAdministers the Agricultural Product Standards Act; sets export standards; acts as the national plant protection organisation for phytosanitary matters, including negotiating market access protocols and issuing phytosanitary certification
PPECBEstablished by the PPECB Act 9 of 1983; controls the export cold chain; acts as assignee for export inspection under the APS Act
Registrar of agricultural remediesRegisters agricultural remedies and fertilisers under Act 36 of 1947
SARS CustomsExport declarations and customs controls
Importing country authoritiesSet and check import requirements, including phytosanitary and residue rules, at the port of entry

Registration requirements

  • Exporter registration with PPECB before exporting regulated products.
  • Food business operator registration for role-players in the export chain, so each can be identified and traced.
  • Production unit codes (PUC) for farms or orchards, and packhouse codes (PHC) for packing facilities.
  • Market-specific registration of orchards, packhouses and cold treatment facilities for markets with bilateral phytosanitary protocols. These registrations often require applications before a set date and audits or pest monitoring during the season.
  • Approved cold stores, containers and vessels for the cold chain.

Registrations must be renewed as required and kept accurate. If a farm changes ownership, adds new blocks or a packhouse moves, the records must be updated. Carton markings depend on these codes, so a wrong or expired code can cause a consignment to fail inspection even when the fruit is perfect.

In practice, the export manager should keep a registration calendar listing every registration, its renewal date, responsible person and the markets it supports, and check it before each season.

lessons.title: The APS Act and PPECB regulatory requirements
lessons.html:
Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990

Objectives: the Act provides for control over the sale and export of certain agricultural products so that defined quality standards are maintained, and for the promotion of those standards. For export, it protects the reputation of South African products and the consumer.

Applicable regulations for fresh produce exports set requirements for each regulated product, typically covering:

  • quality standards, classes and maturity requirements;
  • tolerances for defects per class;
  • packing requirements and container types;
  • marking requirements on each container;
  • sampling and inspection methods;
  • the requirement that regulated products may only be exported after inspection and approval.

Compliance means the producer, packhouse and exporter must know the current standards for each product, pack and mark accordingly, present consignments for inspection, and act on rejections. Standards are amended from time to time, so the business must check that it uses the current version.

Regulatory requirements from the PPECB Act 9 of 1983

  • Registration of exporters of perishable products.
  • Control of the handling, cooling, storage and transport of perishable products intended for export, so that quality is maintained.
  • Approval of facilities and transport, including cold stores, reefer containers and vessels.
  • Payment of statutory levies or fees on exports to fund the Board's services.
  • Compliance with cold chain instructions and temperature regimes set or approved for products and markets.

PPECB's operational role and consequences

PPECB is involved at many steps: it inspects consignments in packhouses and cold stores for APS Act compliance, monitors temperatures, approves containers before loading, oversees cold treatment monitoring for some markets, and issues the certificates the exporter needs. It also collects data on volumes, temperatures and inspection results that the industry uses for planning.

For stakeholders, the consequences are clear. A failed inspection means the consignment cannot be exported as declared and must be reworked, downgraded or redirected. A cold chain failure can invalidate a cold treatment or lead to a claim. Non-payment of levies or non-registration can stop exports altogether. Good cooperation with PPECB, accurate bookings and good presentation of consignments reduce delays and costs.

lessons.title: Phytosanitary regulations and their influence
lessons.html:
What phytosanitary regulations are

Phytosanitary regulations protect plants in the importing country from foreign pests and diseases. They are based on the International Plant Protection Convention (IPPC), under which each country has a national plant protection organisation. In South Africa this function sits with the national Department of Agriculture.

How they work for exporters

  • Pest risk analysis: the importing country assesses the risk posed by each product from South Africa.
  • Market access protocols: for many products and markets, bilateral agreements set out exactly what must be done, such as orchard registration, pest monitoring and control, packhouse procedures, inspection and treatments.
  • Treatments: for example cold treatment against fruit fly or false codling moth, in which pulp temperature must stay below a set limit for a set number of days, or other approved treatments.
  • Inspection and certification: consignments are inspected for pests and, if they comply, a phytosanitary certificate is issued. It must match the consignment exactly.
  • Inspection on arrival: the importing country checks the consignment and the certificate. Interceptions of quarantine pests can lead to rejection, destruction or treatment, and repeated interceptions can lead to suspension of a farm, a packhouse or a whole country's access.

Influence on exports

  • Some markets are open only to registered units that have followed the full protocol for the season.
  • Treatments add cost and can affect fruit quality; cold treatment also lengthens the time before fruit can be sold.
  • Pests such as false codling moth and diseases such as citrus black spot have strongly shaped citrus access to markets like the EU.
  • New market access takes years of negotiation and data, so industry associations and government work together on it.

Managers must plan registrations and pest control programmes a season ahead, keep complete records, and ensure that what is declared on the certificate is exactly what is in the container.

Key points

  • The Department of Agriculture, PPECB and the remedies registrar are key regulators.
  • Exporters, production units and packhouses must be registered and codes kept current.
  • The APS Act sets quality, packing, marking and inspection requirements.
  • The PPECB Act controls the export cold chain, facilities and levies.
  • Phytosanitary protocols decide market access and must be followed exactly.
